chapter_theme: The warrior's pride, spoken largely from within: boast, disdain for easy prey, mercy as courage's edge, and death sought as honour. Its ethic is one of glory and is not softened by the rest of the Kural.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar ties several verses to the conventions of heroic poetry (Purapporul Venba Malai), and groups 777-780 as not cherishing life. Manakkudavar's commentary marks the end of a section at 780.

771.reading: Enemies, do not stand before my lord; many who stood before him now stand in stone.
771.nuance: The verse puns on நில்: to stand in battle and to stand as a hero-stone. The stone is both a threat and an honour, a fact that makes the boast double-edged. It is a voice in the Kural that isn't Valluvar's own, and Parimelazhagar notes the warrior places his valour on his king.

772.reading: Carrying a spear that missed an elephant is sweeter than carrying an arrow that hit a forest hare.
772.nuance: The verse measures an act by its target, not its result. Parimelazhagar supplies a dramatic setting, a warrior ashamed that the opposing force fled, but the verse itself gives only the comparison.

773.reading: They call fierceness great manhood; but when something befalls the foe, generous help is its cutting edge.
773.nuance: The image is exact: the kindness isn't an exception to valour but its sharpest point. Parimelazhagar's example is Rama telling the defeated Ravana to go and come back tomorrow, an epic illustration that the verse doesn't state.

774.reading: Having sent his spear away with an elephant, he comes on seeking another, and laughs as he pulls one from his own body.
774.nuance: The laugh is the verse's whole shock. For Parimelazhagar he is happy because he has found what he was seeking, and rage had kept him from noticing the wound. A wound registers as supply.

775.reading: When the eye that glares at the enemy gives way and blinks at a flung spear, is that not flight, to the fierce?
775.nuance: Valour is carried to the reflex. Parimelazhagar's line is that even withdrawing the angry gaze counts as retreat.

positions.position: The spear is thrown at the man, and giving way means ending the glare by blinking.
positions.quote: அவர் வேலைக்கொண்டு எறிய அஃது ஆற்றாது அந்நோக்கை அழித்து இமைக்குமாயின்

positions.position: The spear is thrust into the eye itself, and blinking again at that is equal to defeat.
positions.quote: மாற்றாரோடு எதிர்த்துச் சிவந்து நோக்கின கண்ணிலே ஒரு வேலினாலே எறிய

776.reading: Going over his days, he sets among the wasted all those on which he took no noble wound.
776.nuance: விழுப்புண் is a wound of a certain kind. Parimelazhagar restricts it to face and chest, so that it marks one who did not turn. A ledger of days is a sober image for a very unsober ethic.

777.reading: For those who want fame that circles the world and do not want life, the tying on of the war-anklet is an adornment.
777.nuance: The verse names only fame. Parimelazhagar adds heaven (துறக்கம்), saying fame remains encircling the earth while the hero goes on, so the afterlife is his reading. காரிகை turns a mark of danger into jewellery.

778.reading: Warriors who do not fear for their lives when battle comes will not lessen in their distinction even if their lord is angry.
778.nuance: This verse makes a real space between warrior and king, which the army chapter's language of loyalty doesn't.

positions.position: They press on to battle even if the king angrily forbids it, because their ardour doesn't diminish.
positions.quote: தம் இறைவன் அது வேண்டா என்று முனியினும் அவ் வீரமிகுதி குன்றார்.

positions.position: The true warriors are those who go on doing their duty though their leader is angry with them.

779.reading: Who could reproach those who die so that what they vowed is not broken, for having failed?
779.nuance: Parimelazhagar makes a bold move: dying in the attempt counts as fulfilling the vow. The verse's rhetorical question closes off blame for one who failed, without calling the failure a success.

780.reading: If one can die so that the eyes of those who sustained one fill with tears, that death is worth begging for.
780.nuance: The measure of the death is another's tears, and the one who weeps is the patron. Parimelazhagar sets it against dying sick at home among weeping kin, which only spends old deeds, whereas this earns heaven. The verse itself mentions neither of those.

links.note: Both use பேராண்மை. Here the word is first attached to fierceness in battle. In 148 the great manhood is not looking at another's wife. The Kural contests what manhood is, and 773's own turn to helping the fallen foe is partway to 148.

Two claims about the sharpest edge (எஃகு). In 759 wealth is the sharpest steel for cutting an enemy's pride. In 773 the edge of valour is helping that enemy when he falls. Cutting and sparing are both called sharpness.

596 says aim high, since even a failure is as good as not failing. 772 gives the warrior's version: the spear that missed an elephant is better than the arrow that hit a hare. Aim outranks outcome in both.

Both judge a life day by day and ask for no wasted days. In 38 the good deed makes a day count, and it blocks future births. In 776 the wound makes a day count. Two complete moral accountings use one form.

1066 says nothing shames the tongue more than begging, even water for a cow. 780 says this death is worth begging for, with the same root (இர-). Only something beyond the Kural's worst disgrace could justify the word.
231 says the only profit for a life is to give and live with fame (இசை). 777 wants the same இசை, and pays for it with life itself. Giving and dying are two routes to one reward.
